clips.text_zh: Cybercab 真係可以買嚟放落 Tesla Robotaxi network 收租？被動收入聽落好正 但實質係點🤔 又係 Elon 隻講故事 唔好信晒 ok
clips.text_en_b1: Redpill me on buying Cybercabs and putting them to work on the Tesla Robotaxi network for passive income. How realistic is it, and what kind of return could a retail buyer actually expect per year?
clips.source_hint: /biz/ thread asking whether buying Cybercabs for the Tesla Robotaxi network is a real passive-income play.

signal.rationale: Implied bullish bet on Tesla Robotaxi narrative and Cybercab unit economics

clips.text_en_b2: Could somebody break down what would actually happen if a retail investor bought a Cybercab and listed it on Tesla's Robotaxi network for passive income? On paper the pitch sounds appealing, yet I remain sceptical because Elon has a track record of overpromising. What realistic annual yield could a small-time buyer genuinely expect once depreciation, maintenance and downtime are factored in? Hard numbers preferred over hype.
clips.text_en_c1: I'm looking for a sober, evidence-based breakdown of the Cybercab investment proposition. Assuming Tesla eventually launches its Robotaxi network and permits individual owners to enrol their vehicles, what realistic annual returns could a retail buyer genuinely anticipate, net of depreciation, insurance, maintenance, and platform fees? The passive-income narrative Musk has been pushing certainly sounds compelling, but projections tend to obscure the underlying assumptions. Before committing capital, I would welcome analysis that separates verifiable milestones from vapourware, and that quantifies the breakeven horizon under conservative utilisation scenarios. In short: is this a credible yield-generating asset, or another exercise in storytelling dressed up as financial planning?
clips.text_en_c2: I would welcome a sober assessment of the proposition that retail investors ought to acquire Cybercabs and subsequently lease them into Tesla's nascent Robotaxi network, thereby cultivating a stream of ostensibly passive revenue. On paper, the narrative is intoxicating: a fleet of autonomous vehicles earning fares while one sleeps, dividends arriving as neatly as quarterly coupons. In practice, however, the entire edifice rests on Musk's customary gift for theatrical announcements rather than verifiable operating metrics. The unit economics remain opaque, regulatory clearance is far from assured, and the discount rate one ought to apply to projected cash flows is, charitably, heroic. Before any retail participant commits capital, they would be well advised to interrogate the assumption that Musk's promises translate, however belatedly, into dependable yield.

clips.text_zh: BTC 同黃金揀一樣揸十年 揀邊樣？其實我兩個都輸緊錢 lol 真係笑死人🙏 不過 long term 一定 BTC 啦 黃金太慢
clips.text_en_b1: Bitcoin vs Gold. If you had to hold only one for the next 10 years, would you choose Bitcoin or gold? What makes your choice better than the other? State your case clearly, no copium.
clips.source_hint: /biz/ debate thread forcing anons to pick Bitcoin or gold for a 10-year hold.

signal.rationale: Anon leans long BTC over gold for the 10-year horizon; XAU framed as the slower alternative

clips.text_en_b2: If you were forced to pick a single asset and hold it for the next decade, would you go with Bitcoin or gold? Make your case clearly, because copium-infused answers will be ignored. Personally I am bleeding on both positions right now, which is honestly comical, but over the long run Bitcoin has to outperform. Gold simply moves too slowly to stay competitive.
clips.text_en_c1: If you were compelled to hold a single asset for the next decade, Bitcoin or gold, which would you select, and on what grounds? I am personally bleeding on both positions, so sentimentality is off the table. What matters is the underlying thesis: scarcity mechanics, monetary policy hedging, demographic demand, and the regulatory tailwinds or headwinds each faces. Gold's volatility profile is undeniably more sedate, yet its growth ceiling appears structurally constrained in a digital economy. Bitcoin, conversely, offers asymmetric upside alongside existential technological risk. Lay out your case methodically, cite whatever evidence you find persuasive, and spare me the copium. Conviction backed by reasoning is what I am after.
clips.text_en_c2: Were one compelled, by some hypothetical exercise in disciplined portfolio construction, to select a single asset to hold for the ensuing decade, the choice between Bitcoin and gold presents a genuinely instructive dilemma. Gold, after all, has endured millennia as a store of value precisely because it is dull: its scarcity is uncontested, its custody straightforward, and its correlation with broader monetary debasement both intuitive and well-documented. Bitcoin, by contrast, promises a far steeper ascent, predicated upon the thesis that programmable scarcity will ultimately eclipse the metal's inertial conservatism. Yet that same volatility cuts both ways, and the asset's notorious drawdowns have a habit of testing the resolve of those who purchased conviction at the peak.

clips.text_zh: 2026年仲有火箭同AI 但打印機仲係廢物一個 紙 Jam 就死 噴頭壞就換機 wtf 我哋做工程嘅真係頂唔順🧐
clips.text_en_b1: Why is there no ThinkPad of printers? It's 2026. We have reusable rockets and powerful AI, yet consumer printers are still brittle, unreliable nightmares. We need tank-like build quality, modular parts, and true repairability. Why hasn't anyone built it?
clips.source_hint: /g/ thread asking why no manufacturer has built a rugged, repairable ThinkPad-style printer.
clips.text_en_b2: Why on earth has nobody produced a ThinkPad equivalent for printers? It is 2026 and we have reusable rockets plus increasingly capable AI, yet consumer printers remain fragile, paper-jamming nightmares with proprietary parts and zero repairability. What engineers genuinely need is tank-like build quality, modular components and proper documentation. The technology clearly exists, so why has nobody bothered to build it?
clips.text_en_c1: It is frankly absurd that, in 2026, we have managed to land reusable orbital boosters and deploy generative AI at scale, yet the humble consumer printer remains a triumph of planned obsolescence. Paper jams, clogged printheads, proprietary cartridges, and driver incompatibilities continue to plague users who simply want reliable output. What the market evidently lacks is a ThinkPad equivalent: a machine engineered with modular components, documented schematics, and rugged construction prioritising repairability over quarterly revenue cycles. Given how mature the underlying technology is, one has to wonder whether the absence reflects genuine engineering difficulty or, more cynically, a coordinated preference among manufacturers for disposable hardware.
clips.text_en_c2: It is, frankly, astonishing that in an era characterised by reusable orbital launch vehicles and language models of startling capability, the consumer printer remains an exercise in engineered obsolescence and quiet user despair. Paper jams, clogged printheads, and proprietary DRM-locked consumables conspire to render a device that should be unremarkable into a recurring source of existential frustration. What the market conspicuously lacks, and what engineering tradition ought to have produced long ago, is a printer conceived along the same philosophical lines as a ThinkPad: robust chassis, modular components, readily available schematics, and a commitment to repairability that extends meaningfully beyond the cosmetic. The economics, one suspects, discourage such an enterprise, since disposability remains the industry's structural profit centre and longevity would, rather inconveniently, cannibalise recurring revenue streams.

clips.text_zh: 內地最新潮流係「泡泡下巴」 女性 influencer 帶起 omg 真係睇唔明 審美觀崩壞中 lol
clips.text_en_b1: Newest trend in China just dropped. Chinese internet users are calling it the bubble chin. It is becoming increasingly fashionable among Chinese female influencers and is spreading fast across lifestyle platforms.
clips.source_hint: /pol/ thread on the new bubble chin cosmetic trend among Chinese female influencers.
clips.text_en_b2: A rather bewildering aesthetic trend has just emerged across Chinese social media, and mainstream commentators are already labelling it the bubble chin. The look appears to have been popularised by lifestyle influencers and is reportedly spreading rapidly across Xiaohongshu and Douyin. Honestly, I struggle to see the appeal, and judging by the reaction threads many locals feel the same way. Standards are clearly slipping.
clips.text_en_c1: The latest aesthetic phenomenon to emerge from Chinese social media is, predictably, bewildering to outside observers. Referred to colloquially as the bubble chin, the trend involves a deliberately exaggerated, softened lower-jaw contour that has been popularised by lifestyle influencers and is now propagating across Xiaohongshu, Douyin, and adjacent platforms at considerable velocity. While the precise origins remain debated, the broader implications are more interesting than the look itself: it illustrates how algorithmic amplification can convert niche beauty standards into mass phenomena within weeks, often detached from any anatomical rationale. Whether this represents genuine aesthetic evolution or merely another cycle of internet-driven homogenisation is, frankly, an open question.
clips.text_en_c2: The latest aesthetic phenomenon to percolate through Chinese social media, colloquially termed the bubble chin, has ascended from niche subcultural curiosity to mainstream trend with remarkable velocity. Propelled by a constellation of female influencers who appear to have collectively decided that an exaggerated, inflated jawline constitutes the apogee of contemporary beauty, the look has proliferated across lifestyle platforms, beauty forums, and short-video applications with an intensity that borders on the missionary. Critics, perhaps predictably, have decried the trend as yet another symptom of aesthetic standards veering toward the absurd, while defenders insist it represents nothing more than playful self-expression.

clips.text_zh: 見個 Fallout 4 帖諗起以前打完又 Gank LOL 嘅日子 廢青中廢青lol btw Fallout 4 真係好game 定overhype？
clips.text_en_b1: Is Fallout 4 really as good as people say it is? When I first played it, it felt like a game that was developed too quickly and rushed to release. Curious how other anons feel about it years later.
clips.source_hint: /v/ thread debating whether Fallout 4 deserved its huge reputation.
clips.text_en_b2: Is Fallout 4 genuinely worth playing today, or has the nostalgia simply clouded our judgement? When I first finished it years ago the whole experience felt rushed, as though Bethesda had pushed it out the door a year too early. The world-building was solid, yet the dialogue system and quest design left a lot to be desired. Curious how other anons rate it now.
clips.text_en_c1: Years after its release, Fallout 4 continues to divide the community in ways that newer titles rarely do. When I first played it, my impression was that Bethesda had clearly prioritised meeting a commercial deadline over delivering a polished experience; quests felt truncated, the dialogue system regressed, and the overall scope suggested a project that could have benefited from another twelve months in development. Revisiting it now, however, I am inclined to reassess. The modding ecosystem has matured considerably, the gunplay holds up reasonably well, and the world-building, while not on par with New Vegas, retains that distinctive Bethesda charm.
clips.text_en_c2: The question of whether Fallout 4 genuinely merits the canonical status so routinely bestowed upon it is one that has, in the years since its release, occasioned a great deal of spirited disagreement. Initial impressions among a substantial contingent of players were coloured by a pervasive sense that the title had been hurried through production, with compromises evident in dialogue systems, settlement mechanics, and a main questline that, frankly, felt somewhat vestigial. Yet subsequent playthroughs, particularly those undertaken after the Commonwealth has been properly explored and its factions fully engaged, tend to rehabilitate the title's reputation considerably. The world, for all its technical roughness, possesses a peculiar density, and the radiantly bleak humour endures.

clips.text_zh: 肥仔信成日話我 bench 太重 grap 太廢 又話被人 50lb 細佬打到仆街 lol 我信佢啦🧐 真係要開始練 BJJ
clips.text_en_b1: Hey nice bench press anon, 315 lbs really impressive. Any guy who weighs 50 pounds less than you can fold you in half on the ground. You have no reason to skip grappling, unless you want some smaller dude to make you his bitch. Take the grappling pill.
clips.source_hint: /fit/ thread telling lifters they are skipping grappling and getting humbled by lighter opponents.

signal.rationale: Fitness / martial arts advice, no trade

clips.text_en_b2: Solid bench press, although bragging about lifting 315 pounds is frankly meaningless when any training partner weighing fifty pounds less can absolutely demolish you on the mats. Strength built in one plane does not transfer to live grappling, and that competitive gap becomes painfully obvious the moment you are taken down. Unless you genuinely enjoy being controlled by smaller opponents, start training Brazilian jiu-jitsu today.
clips.text_en_c1: Credit where it is due: a 315-pound bench press is objectively impressive and speaks to consistent, disciplined training. That said, strength metrics performed in a single plane of motion translate poorly to scenarios where the fight, quite literally, hits the ground. Any competent grappler weighing significantly less than you can, with minimal effort, neutralise that strength advantage through leverage, positional control, and technique refined over years of live sparring. The uncomfortable truth is that muscle mass, however aesthetic, is no substitute for grappling literacy. If your goal is functional self-defence rather than mirror aesthetics, Brazilian jiu-jitsu deserves a serious place in your programming.
clips.text_en_c2: Compliments to the anonymous individual whose bench press numbers are, by any reasonable standard, genuinely formidable; 315 pounds is not a feat to be dismissed. Strength, however, is not a unidimensional virtue, and the inflexibly linear worship of axial loading obscures a rather fundamental truth about combative reality: a man forty or fifty pounds lighter, provided he has invested even a modest portion of his training in Brazilian jiu-jitsu, can, with contemptuous ease, escort such a benched behemoth to the floor and there proceed to illustrate, through empirical demonstration, the perils of neglecting one's grappling curriculum. The illusion of dominance, so carefully cultivated beneath the barbell, dissolves with embarrassing speed the moment the contest transitions to horizontal entanglement.

clips.text_zh: 一試真fans就知 Fairy Tail 唔計Lucy 即刻講個角色名 Erza ok🙏 我哋 Gundam 00 / 鬼滅 / Attack on Titan 老粉不要戰
clips.text_en_b1: If you are a true anime fan, mention one Fairy Tail character off the bat that is not Lucy. Go. Bonus points if you can also name a Demon Slayer hashira and a Gundam 00 pilot without Googling them.
clips.source_hint: /a/ thread testing who is actually a real anime fan via Fairy Tail trivia.
clips.text_en_b2: A quick litmus test for self-proclaimed anime fans: name a Fairy Tail character other than Lucy immediately, and you have thirty seconds to do it. Erza is the obvious pick, yet plenty of viewers would draw a blank. For extra credit, identify a Demon Slayer hashira and a Gundam 00 pilot without resorting to Google. Anyone who passes clearly belongs to the veteran fanbase.
clips.text_en_c1: A quick litmus test for anyone claiming genuine long-term investment in anime as a medium: name, without hesitation, a Fairy Tail character who is not Lucy Heartfilia. Erza Scarlet is the obvious candidate, though Natsu or Gray would equally suffice. Should you wish to demonstrate broader credentials, extending the exercise to identify a Demon Slayer hashira and a Gundam 00 pilot from memory would be considerably more persuasive. The underlying point is not gatekeeping for its own sake; rather, it distinguishes casual viewers from those whose engagement spans years and franchises. If those references landed instantly, you have likely earned the title of veteran.
clips.text_en_c2: A modest proposal for distinguishing the genuine aficionado from the casual dilettante, the sort of test that separates those who have actually imbibed a series from those who have merely absorbed its cultural residue. Name, without recourse to external prompting, a Fairy Tail character who is not Lucy Heartfilia: should Erza Scarlet spring forth with appropriate alacrity, one may cautiously proceed. Should the respondent stumble and offer, say, a vague reference to Natsu, they may yet be redeemed by extending the inquiry to a Hashira from Demon Slayer, perhaps Giyu Tomioka or the incandescent Shinobu Kocho, and subsequently a Gundam 00 pilot, of whom Setsuna F. Seiei remains the perennial favourite.
